milky-way.name: Milky Way
milky-way.introduction: is our home galaxy, a barred spiral about 87,000 light-years across with 100–400 billion stars. The Sun lies about 27,000 light-years from its center, which hides behind thick dust in Sagittarius. Seen from inside, the disk wraps around the sky as a hazy band of light.

image.alt: The band of the Milky Way across the sky, with dark dust lanes over the bright Galactic Center.
image.caption: ESO/S. Brunier · visible-light all-sky mosaic · released 2009
image.credit: ESO/S. Brunier. Visible-light all-sky mosaic, released 2009. Cropped to the central 120° × 60° around the Galactic Center, resized to 600 × 300 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: ESO: The Milky Way panorama

sections.title: One galaxy among many
sections.text: Galileo Galilei first resolved the hazy band into individual stars with his telescope in 1610. Until the early 1920s, most astronomers thought the Milky Way held every star in the universe. After the 1920 Great Debate between Harlow Shapley and Heber Curtis, observations by Edwin Hubble in 1923 showed that it is just one of many galaxies.

sections.title: A black hole at the heart
sections.text: At the center sits the radio source Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole of about 4.1 million solar masses. The Event Horizon Telescope imaged its shadow in radio waves, published in 2022. Around it, the innermost 10,000 light-years hold a bulge of mostly old stars, from which the galaxy’s bar extends.

sections.title: Measured by a single star
sections.text: The star S2 circles Sagittarius A* every 16 years on a long, narrow orbit. Astronomers followed it for 27 years, and from 2017 the GRAVITY instrument measured its offset from the black hole to as little as 20 millionths of an arcsecond. Its orbit puts the center 8,178 parsecs away, about 26,700 light-years, to 0.3%.

source.title: GRAVITY Collaboration (2019): A geometric distance measurement to the Galactic center black hole with 0.3% uncertainty

sections.title: One lap in 212 million years
sections.text: Stars away from the bulge and the outer rim orbit the center at 200–220 km/s, almost regardless of their distance from it. The Sun takes about 212 million years for one lap.

large-magellanic-cloud.name: Large Magellanic Cloud
large-magellanic-cloud.introduction: is the largest satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, about 162,000 light-years away across Dorado and Mensa. To the naked eye it is a faint cloud about 10° long, 20 times the Moon’s diameter. It holds the Tarantula Nebula, the most active star-forming region in the Local Group.

image.alt: The Large Magellanic Cloud: a bright bluish bar of stars with pink star-forming nebulae above it.
image.caption: CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/SMASH/D. Nidever (Montana State University) · SMASH survey · released 2020
image.credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/SMASH/D. Nidever (Montana State University). Image processing: Travis Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage), Mahdi Zamani and Davide de Martin. Released 2020. Cropped to the galaxy, resized to 600 × 349 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: NOIRLab: Deepest, widest view of the Large Magellanic Cloud from SMASH

sections.title: Bound for the Milky Way
sections.text: The bar at its center suggests that the cloud was once a barred dwarf spiral, until the pull of the Small Magellanic Cloud and the Milky Way disrupted its arms. Its story is not over: the Large Magellanic Cloud is predicted to merge with the Milky Way in about 2.4 billion years.

sections.title: Heavy enough to bend a stream
sections.text: The Orphan stream is a long trail of stars orbiting the Milky Way. Its stars move at an angle to the trail, a sign of a large gravitational kick. Modeling that kick weighs the Large Magellanic Cloud at about 140 billion solar masses, dark matter included, enough to disturb other structures orbiting the Milky Way.

source.title: Erkal et al. (2019): The total mass of the Large Magellanic Cloud from its perturbation on the Orphan stream

sections.title: The cosmic yardstick’s anchor
sections.text: Cepheid variable stars measure distances to other galaxies, but they must first be calibrated in a galaxy whose distance is known. The Large Magellanic Cloud has long been that anchor. In 2019, eclipsing binaries of cool late-type stars measured its distance to 1%, a key step toward a 1% value of the Hubble constant.

source.title: Pietrzyński et al. (2019): A distance to the Large Magellanic Cloud that is precise to one per cent

sections.title: Two bright Canopi
sections.text: A claimed mention by the Persian astronomer al-Sufi around 964 seems to refer to other stars. The first confirmed record is a letter by Amerigo Vespucci from 1502, which mentions “three Canopi, two bright and one obscure”: the two Magellanic Clouds and the dark Coalsack. Ferdinand Magellan saw the cloud on his 1519 voyage, and it now bears his name.

sections.title: A celestial treasure house
sections.text: Rich in gas and dust, the cloud is still forming stars at a brisk pace. Surveys have found about 60 globular clusters, 400 planetary nebulae and 700 open clusters, along with hundreds of thousands of giant and supergiant stars. Supernova 1987A, the nearest supernova in recent years, exploded here.

small-magellanic-cloud.name: Small Magellanic Cloud
small-magellanic-cloud.introduction: is a dwarf galaxy orbiting the Milky Way, about 204,000 light-years away across Tucana and part of Hydrus. It is one of the most distant objects visible to the naked eye, a faint hazy patch about 4.2° across, eight times the Moon’s width. Its Cepheid stars gave astronomers their first ruler for the universe.

image.alt: The Small Magellanic Cloud: a bluish, irregular cloud of stars with pink star-forming nebulae.
image.caption: CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/SMASH/D. Nidever (Montana State University) · SMASH survey · released 2020
image.credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/SMASH/D. Nidever (Montana State University). Image processing: Travis Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage), Mahdi Zamani and Davide de Martin. Released 2020. Resized to 600 × 500 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: NOIRLab: Deepest, widest view of the Small Magellanic Cloud from SMASH

sections.title: The ruler for the universe
sections.text: Henrietta Swan Leavitt at Harvard studied photographic plates of the cloud taken in Arequipa, Peru. In 1908 she published that the variable stars now called Cepheids brighten and fade on periods that follow their brightness. Because all of the cloud’s stars lie at about the same distance, this meant a link between period and true luminosity: Cepheids became standard candles.

sections.title: Deeper than it is wide
sections.text: Fifteen eclipsing binaries measured the cloud’s distance to better than 2%. They also revealed its shape: the binaries form an elongated structure, steeply tilted to the sky. The nearest and the farthest system differ by 10 kiloparsecs, about 33,000 light-years, along the line of sight.

source.title: Graczyk et al. (2020): A distance determination to the Small Magellanic Cloud with an accuracy of better than two percent

sections.title: Two clouds in one?
sections.text: One study proposed that a past encounter with the Large Magellanic Cloud split the small cloud, and named the smaller piece the Mini Magellanic Cloud. In 2023, another found two separate structures with distinct chemical compositions in their stars and gas, about 5 kiloparsecs apart.

sections.title: A bridge to its big sister
sections.text: A bridge of gas, where new stars are forming, links the Small Magellanic Cloud to the Large one, evidence of their tidal pull on each other. The two share an envelope of hydrogen gas, a sign that they have been bound together for a long time. The small cloud’s central bar hints that it, too, was once a barred spiral.

andromeda-galaxy.name: Andromeda Galaxy
andromeda-galaxy.introduction: is the nearest large spiral galaxy and the largest member of the Local Group, about 2.5 million light-years away in Andromeda. At magnitude 3.4 it is visible to the naked eye on moonless nights, even under moderate light pollution. Also known as Messier 31 or NGC 224, it is moving toward the Milky Way.

image.alt: The Andromeda Galaxy seen at a steep angle, with a bright yellowish core, dark dust lanes and its two small companion galaxies.
image.caption: Adam Evans · visible light with hydrogen-alpha · 2010
image.credit: Adam Evans. Visible light with a hydrogen-alpha layer, 2010. Resized to 600 × 394 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: Andromeda Galaxy (with h-alpha)

sections.title: The little cloud
sections.text: Around 964, the Persian astronomer al-Sufi described a “small cloud” in his Book of Fixed Stars. It is the first known reference to a galaxy other than the Milky Way, and star charts of the period labeled it the Little Cloud.

sections.title: Proof of other galaxies
sections.text: Whether the “Great Andromeda Nebula” lay inside the Milky Way was long disputed. In 1922, Ernst Öpik estimated from the speeds of its stars that it lay far outside. Edwin Hubble settled the debate in 1925: on photographs taken with the 100-inch Hooker telescope he found Cepheid variables, whose distance showed an entirely separate galaxy.

sections.title: Collision course?
sections.text: Andromeda approaches the Milky Way at about 110 km/s, one of only about 100 galaxies seen with a blueshift. Once its sideways motion was measured, a direct collision was predicted in about 4 billion years. Later calculations with Gaia data and the pull of other Local Group galaxies gave a much lower chance: about 50% in the next 10 billion years.

sections.title: A ring of fire
sections.text: Its gas and dust lie in several overlapping rings. The most prominent, 32,000 light-years from the core, is nicknamed the ring of fire. Made mainly of cold dust, it hides from visible light, yet most of the galaxy’s star formation happens there. Infrared images from Spitzer show two segmented spiral arms emerging from a central bar.

sections.title: Measured to 1.5%
sections.text: Hubble Space Telescope observations of 55 Cepheids, in the same three filters used to calibrate them in the Large Magellanic Cloud, give a distance of 761,000 parsecs, about 2.48 million light-years, uncertain by just 1.5%.

source.title: Li et al. (2021): A Sub-2% Distance to M31 from Photometrically Homogeneous Near-infrared Cepheid Period–Luminosity Relations

triangulum-galaxy.name: Triangulum Galaxy
triangulum-galaxy.introduction: is a spiral galaxy about 2.7 million light-years away in Triangulum, the third-largest member of the Local Group after the Andromeda Galaxy and the Milky Way. Under a truly dark sky, some people can just see it without optical aid, which makes it the most distant permanent object visible to the naked eye. It is also known as Messier 33 or NGC 598.

image.alt: The Triangulum Galaxy seen nearly face-on, with loose spiral arms dotted by pink star-forming regions.
image.caption: T. A. Rector (NRAO/AUI/NSF and NOIRLab/NSF/AURA) and M. Hanna (NOIRLab/NSF/AURA) · Kitt Peak 0.9-meter telescope
image.credit: T. A. Rector (NRAO/AUI/NSF and NOIRLab/NSF/AURA) and M. Hanna (NOIRLab/NSF/AURA). Taken with the 0.9-meter telescope on Kitt Peak and the NOAO Mosaic camera. Resized to 600 × 612 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: M33, NGC 598

sections.title: The first galaxy seen to turn
sections.text: In 2005, radio astronomers tracked two water masers on opposite sides of the galaxy with the Very Long Baseline Array. For the first time, they could measure a galaxy’s rotation and its motion across the sky directly. It moves at about 190 km/s relative to the Milky Way, toward the Andromeda Galaxy, of which it may be a satellite.

sections.title: A nursery 1,500 light-years wide
sections.text: Northeast of the core lies NGC 604, one of the largest H II regions known, nearly 1,500 light-years across, with a spectrum similar to the Orion Nebula’s. William Herschel listed it separately from the galaxy, and it later received its own NGC number.

sections.title: Hubble’s other Cepheids
sections.text: In 1922–23, John Charles Duncan and Max Wolf found variable stars in the galaxy. In 1926, Edwin Hubble showed that 35 of them were Cepheids and estimated their distance, more evidence that spiral nebulae are galaxies of their own.

sections.title: A stream to Andromeda
sections.text: In 2004, astronomers announced a clumpy stream of hydrogen gas linking the Triangulum and Andromeda galaxies, a hint that the two have pulled on each other in the past. The discovery was confirmed in 2011.

sections.title: Measured to 1.3%
sections.text: Hubble Space Telescope photometry of 154 Cepheids, calibrated against the Large Magellanic Cloud, puts the galaxy 840,000 parsecs away, about 2.74 million light-years, with an uncertainty of just 1.3%.

source.title: Breuval et al. (2023): A 1.3% Distance to M33 from Hubble Space Telescope Cepheid Photometry

sagittarius-dwarf-galaxy.name: Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy
sagittarius-dwarf-galaxy.introduction: is a dwarf galaxy being torn apart by the Milky Way, about 86,000 light-years away in Sagittarius, on the far side of the Galactic Center. Also called the Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy, it was the nearest known galaxy when it was found in 1994. Its stars trail along a stream that loops around the whole Milky Way.

image.alt: A grey map of star density: the bright band of the Milky Way across the top, the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy outlined as a faint vertical streak below the Galactic Center, and the two Magellanic Clouds at lower right.
image.caption: ESA/Gaia/DPAC · map of star density from Gaia · released 2018
image.credit: ESA/Gaia/DPAC. All-sky map of the density of stars observed by Gaia from July 2014 to May 2016, released 2018. Cropped to the region below the Galactic Center, resized to 600 × 375 and converted to AVIF; the label and outline are part of the original.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: The Sagittarius dwarf galaxy in Gaia’s all-sky view

sections.title: Hidden behind the Galactic Center
sections.text: Rodrigo Ibata, Mike Irwin and Gerry Gilmore discovered the galaxy in 1994. Although it is one of the closest companions of the Milky Way, it lies on the opposite side of the Galactic Center from Earth. Because of this, it is very faint, even though it covers a large area of the sky.

sections.title: Ripples in the Milky Way
sections.text: In 2018, Gaia’s census of more than a billion stars showed that the dwarf galaxy had set stars near the Milky Way’s core rippling as it passed through between 300 and 900 million years ago. A simulation published in 2011 even suggested that repeated collisions with it gave the Milky Way its spiral structure.

sections.title: A loop around the Galaxy
sections.text: In 2003, Steven Majewski, Michael Skrutskie and Martin Weinberg used infrared data from the 2MASS survey to map the full, loop-shaped galaxy. It stands nearly at right angles to the Milky Way’s disk, on a polar orbit that has carried it through the disk several times. One model puts each orbit at 550–750 million years, swinging between about 13 and 41 kiloparsecs from the center.

sections.title: Swallowed within a billion years
sections.text: The galaxy’s main body will pass through the Milky Way’s disk within the next hundred million years. The Milky Way, about 10,000 times as massive, is slowly absorbing it, and its main body is expected to dissolve into the stream of stars it leaves behind within a billion years.

sections.title: A cluster known first
sections.text: The globular cluster M54, known long before the galaxy, appears to sit at its core, and Terzan 7, Terzan 8 and Arp 2 lie in its main body. Palomar 12, NGC 2419 and other clusters travel along its streams. Analyses of VVV and Gaia data have found at least twenty more, mostly richer in metals than the clusters known before.

fornax-dwarf-galaxy.name: Fornax Dwarf Galaxy
fornax-dwarf-galaxy.introduction: is a dwarf spheroidal galaxy orbiting the Milky Way, about 465,000 light-years away in Fornax. It holds six globular clusters, an unusually high number for its size, and the largest of them, NGC 1049, was discovered before the galaxy itself.

image.alt: A faint, bluish haze of countless stars filling the middle of a star field.
image.caption: ESO/Digitized Sky Survey 2 · visible light · released 2010
image.credit: ESO/Digitized Sky Survey 2. Visible-light survey composite, released 2010. Resized to 600 × 600 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: ESO: The Fornax dwarf galaxy

sections.title: Found from South Africa
sections.text: Harlow Shapley discovered the galaxy in 1938 on photographic plates taken with the 24-inch (61 cm) Bruce refractor at Boyden Observatory in South Africa, shortly after he had discovered the Sculptor Dwarf Galaxy.

sections.title: Clusters out of step
sections.text: Hubble observations show that the cluster Fornax 4 is about 3 billion years younger than Fornax 1, 2, 3 and 5. Fornax 6 was long debated as a chance alignment, until a 2021 study confirmed it as a member, richer in metals and therefore likely younger than the others. Why small galaxies like this one kept forming globular clusters long after the Milky Way’s halo had stopped is unknown.

sculptor-dwarf-galaxy.name: Sculptor Dwarf Galaxy
sculptor-dwarf-galaxy.introduction: is a dwarf spheroidal galaxy orbiting the Milky Way, about 274,000 light-years away in Sculptor. Its stars hold only about 4% as much carbon and other heavy elements as the Milky Way, which makes it similar to the primitive galaxies seen near the edge of the observable universe.

image.alt: A thin haze of faint stars spread across most of the frame, with a few brighter foreground stars.
image.caption: ESO · MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, Wide Field Imager · released 2015
image.credit: ESO. Visible-light image taken with the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla, released 2015. Resized to 600 × 549 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: ESO: Sculptor dwarf galaxy

sections.title: The most pristine star outside the Milky Way
sections.text: The galaxy is home to AS0039, the most metal-poor star known outside the Milky Way, with an iron abundance of [Fe/H] = −4.11, less than a ten-thousandth of the Sun’s. Unlike other stars this poor in metals, it holds little carbon. Its unusual mix of elements suggests that it formed after a hypernova of one of the first-generation Population III stars.

sections.title: Two populations, one merger?
sections.text: Its stars fall into two groups, one with [Fe/H] = −2.3 and one with −1.5, and the older, more metal-poor group spreads farther out. Cosmological simulations suggest that the two populations are the sign of a past merger with a smaller companion galaxy.

sections.title: From a 1937 plate to 3D motions
sections.text: Harlow Shapley discovered the galaxy in 1937 with the 24-inch Bruce refractor at Boyden Observatory. Today, Hubble and Gaia observations taken 12 years apart map about 100 of its stars precisely and reveal the motions of about 10 of them in all three dimensions.

draco-dwarf-galaxy.name: Draco Dwarf Galaxy
draco-dwarf-galaxy.introduction: is a dwarf spheroidal galaxy orbiting the Milky Way, about 266,000 light-years away in Draco. It is one of the faintest companions of the Milky Way, yet its stars move so fast that a large amount of dark matter must hold it together.

image.alt: A loose swarm of faint stars, slightly denser in the middle of a dark star field.
image.caption: NASA, ESA, Digitized Sky Survey, R. van der Marel (STScI) · visible light · released 2024
image.credit: NASA, ESA, Digitized Sky Survey, Roeland van der Marel (STScI). Released 2024. Cropped to the wide-field panel of a three-panel image, resized to 600 × 600 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: ESA/Hubble: Draco dwarf galaxy

sections.title: Ruled by dark matter
sections.text: The speeds of its individual stars spread widely, which implies far more mass than its stars provide. Stars torn from a disrupted galaxy could also move this fast, but the galaxy’s narrow horizontal branch does not support that idea. This made Draco the most dark-matter-dominated object known as of 2007.

sections.title: Hubble’s 18-year watch
sections.text: In 2024, astronomers used 18 years of Hubble data to measure how its stars move across the sky. Draco became the first dwarf galaxy whose three-dimensional velocity spread has been measured at different distances from its center. Its dark matter distribution agrees better with the standard cosmological model, easing the cusp–core problem.

sections.title: Hundreds of variable stars
sections.text: In 1961, Walter Baade and Henrietta Swope found over 260 variable stars in the galaxy. Of the 138 near its center, all but five are RR Lyrae stars, whose brightness put the galaxy 81 kiloparsecs away, close to today’s value.

sections.title: Found on Palomar plates
sections.text: Albert George Wilson of Lowell Observatory discovered the galaxy in 1954 on plates of the National Geographic Society – Palomar Observatory Sky Survey. Most of its stars are more than 10 billion years old, and it holds almost no gas or dust.

ursa-minor-dwarf-galaxy.name: Ursa Minor Dwarf Galaxy
ursa-minor-dwarf-galaxy.introduction: is a dwarf spheroidal galaxy orbiting the Milky Way, about 229,000 light-years away in Ursa Minor. Its stars formed in a single burst around 14 billion years ago, so the galaxy is probably as old as the Milky Way itself.

image.alt: An elongated swarm of faint stars crossing a field of brighter foreground stars.
image.caption: Giuseppe Donatiello · composite of public survey data · 2018
image.credit: Giuseppe Donatiello. Composite of public survey data, 2018. Resized to 600 × 600 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: Ursa Minor Dwarf

sections.title: A fossil galaxy
sections.text: In 1999, Kenneth Mighell and Christopher Burke used the Hubble Space Telescope to confirm that the galaxy had a simple history: a single burst of star formation that lasted around 2 billion years. Old stars make up most of it, and it forms few or no new stars today.

sections.title: A find of the Palomar Sky Survey
sections.text: A. G. Wilson of Lowell Observatory discovered the galaxy in 1955, during the Palomar Sky Survey.

carina-dwarf-galaxy.name: Carina Dwarf Galaxy
carina-dwarf-galaxy.introduction: is a dwarf spheroidal galaxy orbiting the Milky Way, about 344,000 light-years away in Carina. Found only in 1977, it formed its stars in bursts billions of years apart, and the Milky Way’s tides are pulling it apart.

image.alt: Many faint stars scattered across the center of a star field, hard to tell from foreground stars.
image.caption: ESO/G. Bono & CTIO · visible light · released 2011
image.credit: ESO/G. Bono & CTIO. Visible light from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope and the Víctor M. Blanco 4-metre telescope, released 2011. Resized to 600 × 500 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: ESO: Hiding in plain sight — the elusive Carina dwarf galaxy

sections.title: A master of camouflage
sections.text: Although it is one of the closest galaxies to Earth, it is so dim and diffuse that astronomers found it only in the 1970s. Its stars are faint and sparse, so it is easy to see right through it, and they are hard to tell apart from foreground stars and distant galaxies. Yet it spans just under half the width of the full Moon.

source.title: ESO: Hiding in plain sight — the elusive Carina dwarf galaxy

sections.title: Three bursts of star birth
sections.text: Cannon and colleagues discovered the galaxy in 1977 with the UK Schmidt Telescope. Most of its stars formed about 7 billion years ago, but it also had bursts of star formation about 13 and 3 billion years ago.

sextans-dwarf-galaxy.name: Sextans Dwarf Galaxy
sextans-dwarf-galaxy.introduction: is a dwarf spheroidal galaxy orbiting the Milky Way, about 280,000 light-years away in Sextans. Its stars are spread so thinly that it was found only in 1990, as the eighth known satellite of the Milky Way.

image.alt: A field of faint stars; the galaxy’s thinly spread stars barely stand out from the foreground.
image.caption: Giuseppe Donatiello · visible light · 2016
image.credit: Giuseppe Donatiello, 2016. Cropped to remove a label, resized to 600 × 600 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: LG Sextans I

sections.title: The eighth satellite
sections.text: Mike Irwin, Peter Bunclark, Mick Bridgeland and Richard McMahon discovered the galaxy in 1990. Its light is spread more thinly than that of any other galaxy on the map: within its half-light radius, each square arcsecond shines only like a star of magnitude 28.

sections.title: Poor in metals
sections.text: Like other dwarf spheroidal galaxies, it consists of old, metal-poor stars. In one study, most had iron abundances between [Fe/H] = −3.2 and −1.4, that is 0.06–4% of the Sun’s. An analysis of several of its stars found all but one of them short of barium.

leo-i-dwarf-galaxy.name: Leo I Dwarf Galaxy
leo-i-dwarf-galaxy.introduction: is a dwarf spheroidal galaxy about 842,000 light-years away in Leo, one of the most distant satellites of the Milky Way. It lies only a third of a degree from Regulus, the brightest star in Leo, and is also called the Regulus Dwarf.

image.alt: The bright blue star Regulus, with the faint, grainy patch of the galaxy just above it.
image.caption: Giuseppe Donatiello · visible light
image.credit: Giuseppe Donatiello. Cropped to Regulus and the galaxy, resized to 600 × 480 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: Regulus and Leo I dwarf

sections.title: In the glare of Regulus
sections.text: Albert George Wilson discovered the galaxy in 1950 on plates of the Palomar Observatory Sky Survey, taken with the 48-inch Schmidt camera. Scattered light from Regulus makes it hard to study, and it was not seen by eye until the 1990s. A sighting usually takes a telescope of 15 cm or more and a dark sky, but in April 2013 one observer reported seeing it through a 7 cm refractor.

sections.title: The youngest of its kind
sections.text: Between 70% and 80% of its stars formed between 6 and 2 billion years ago, and there is little sign of stars older than 10 billion years. About a billion years ago, star formation almost stopped, roughly when the galaxy last passed closest to the Milky Way, which probably stripped its gas. Leo I is thought to be the youngest dwarf spheroidal satellite of the Milky Way.

sections.title: A black hole in a dwarf?
sections.text: One study of its stars’ motions suggested a black hole of three million solar masses at its center, comparable to Sagittarius A*. Another could not confirm it and allows at most a few hundred thousand solar masses. Among the classical dwarf spheroidal satellites of the Milky Way, Leo I has the densest dark matter.

leo-ii-dwarf-galaxy.name: Leo II Dwarf Galaxy
leo-ii-dwarf-galaxy.introduction: is a dwarf spheroidal galaxy about 681,000 light-years away in Leo, one of the more distant satellites of the Milky Way. Also known as Leo B, it consists largely of old stars poor in metals.

image.alt: A round, grainy cloud of faint stars in the middle of a star field.
image.caption: Giuseppe Donatiello · visible light · 2016
image.credit: Giuseppe Donatiello, 2016. Cropped to remove a label, resized to 600 × 600 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: LG Leo II

sections.title: 82,252 stars in two nights
sections.text: In 2007, a team of 15 astronomers observed the galaxy with the 8.2-meter Subaru telescope on Mauna Kea for 90 minutes over two nights and detected 82,252 stars, down to magnitude 26. Most are old and poor in metals, a sign that the galaxy has escaped the galactic cannibalism by which large galaxies such as the Milky Way grow.

sections.title: Found in 1950
sections.text: Robert George Harrington and Albert George Wilson of the Mount Wilson and Palomar Observatories discovered the galaxy in 1950.

messier-32.name: Messier 32
messier-32.introduction: is a compact elliptical galaxy and satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away in Andromeda. Also known as M32 and NGC 221, it is the prototype of the rare compact ellipticals: half of its stars are packed into its inner core.

image.alt: A bright, smooth, yellowish oval of stars in front of the dusty disk of the Andromeda Galaxy.
image.caption: NASA, ESA, B. Williams, Z. Chen, L. C. Johnson; processing J. DePasquale (STScI) · Hubble · released 2025
image.credit: NASA, ESA, Benjamin F. Williams (University of Washington), Zhuo Chen (University of Washington), L. Clifton Johnson (Northwestern University); image processing Joseph DePasquale (STScI). Crop of Hubble’s panorama of the Andromeda Galaxy, released 2025. Resized to 600 × 640 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: Wikimedia Commons: M32 crop of Hubble’s panoramic view of the Andromeda Galaxy

sections.title: A crowded heart
sections.text: Toward its center, the density of stars climbs steeply, past 30 million solar masses per cubic parsec at the smallest radii Hubble can resolve. In the middle sits a supermassive black hole of 1.5–5 million solar masses, and a faint radio and X-ray source there, M32*, is thought to be gas falling into it.

sections.title: In front of Andromeda
sections.text: The measured distances of the two galaxies agree within their uncertainties, but several clues place M32 in front of the Andromeda Galaxy. Its stars and planetary nebulae are not dimmed or reddened by gas or dust, and at the end of November 2000, a star in M32 briefly magnified a star in Andromeda by gravitational microlensing.

sections.title: Leftover of a lost galaxy?
sections.text: How M32 became so compact is unclear. Andromeda’s tides may have stripped a small disk galaxy down to its dense center. Another idea makes it the remnant of a larger spiral, M32p, that merged with Andromeda about two billion years ago. A similar compact elliptical found far from any large galaxy suggests that M32 may simply have been born compact.

messier-110.name: Messier 110
messier-110.introduction: is a dwarf elliptical galaxy and satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy, about 2.7 million light-years away in Andromeda. Also known as M110 and NGC 205, it became the 110th and last object of the Messier catalog almost two centuries after Charles Messier first saw it.

image.alt: A dense field of reddish stars that brightens toward the galaxy’s core at right, with a dark patch of dust.
image.caption: ESA/Hubble & NASA, L. Ferrarese et al. · Hubble · released 2019
image.credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, L. Ferrarese et al. Released 2019. Resized to 600 × 450 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: ESA/Hubble: Not so dead after all

sections.title: On Messier’s drawing
sections.text: Charles Messier never listed the galaxy, but he drew it, together with M32, on his sketch of the Andromeda Galaxy; a label says he first saw it in 1773. Caroline Herschel discovered it independently on 27 August 1783, and her brother William described her discovery in 1785. In 1967, Kenneth Glyn Jones proposed giving it a Messier number.

sections.title: Dust and young stars
sections.text: Its class, pec dE5, marks a dwarf elliptical flattened by 50% that is peculiar: patches of dust and young blue stars lie near its center, which is unusual for its kind and still unexplained. Unlike M32, it shows no sign of a supermassive black hole.

sections.title: Leader of a lost group?
sections.text: About half of the Andromeda Galaxy’s satellites orbit it in a single plane, and 14 of 16 of them go around in the same direction. One model proposes that these 16 once belonged to a group around M110, broken up when it passed close to Andromeda.

ngc-185.name: NGC 185
ngc-185.introduction: is a dwarf elliptical galaxy and satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy, about 2.1 million light-years away in Cassiopeia. Unlike most galaxies of its kind, it holds young star clusters, and its active nucleus may make it the closest Seyfert galaxy to Earth. It is also known as Caldwell 18.

sections.title: The Local Group’s only Seyfert?
sections.text: NGC 185 has an active galactic nucleus and is usually classified as a type II Seyfert galaxy, although that status is questioned. If it holds, NGC 185 is possibly the closest Seyfert galaxy to Earth and the only known one in the Local Group.

sections.title: Young stars at the center
sections.text: Most of its stars formed early, but over the last billion years stars have formed only near its center. Walter Baade found young blue objects there in 1951, which turned out to be star clusters rather than single stars. A supernova remnant lies near the center, too.

sections.title: Catalogued three times
sections.text: William Herschel discovered the galaxy on 30 November 1787 and listed it as H II.707. John Herschel listed it as h 35 in 1833 and as GC 90 in his General Catalogue of 1864. James Keeler first photographed it between 1898 and 1900 with the Crossley Reflector at Lick Observatory.

ngc-147.name: NGC 147
ngc-147.introduction: is a dwarf elliptical galaxy and satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy, about 2.4 million light-years away in Cassiopeia. It forms a physical pair with NGC 185 but is fainter and slightly larger, so its light is spread more thinly and it is harder to see. It is also known as Caldwell 17.

sections.title: Resolved into stars
sections.text: John Herschel discovered the galaxy in September 1829. In 1944, Walter Baade resolved it into individual stars with the telescope at Mount Wilson, which confirmed that it belongs to the Local Group.

sections.title: Where did the gas go?
sections.text: Its last significant burst of star formation took place around 3 billion years ago. Its stars differ in metallicity, so earlier generations enriched its gas, yet no neutral hydrogen has been found, and the limit on its gas is far below what its aging stars should have returned.
